standard_text: Develop probability models that include the sample space and probabilities of outcomes to represent simple events with equally likely outcomes. Predict the approximate relative frequency of the event based on the model. Compare probabilities from the model to observed frequencies, evaluate the level of agreement, and explain possible sources of discrepancy.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to build a probability model with its sample space, use the model to predict how often an event should happen, and then compare the model's probabilities to what an experiment actually produced. The on-grade skills climb from assigning 1/n in a uniform model, to reading a model, to favorable over total from a sample space, to predicting counts over N trials, to computing experimental probability from real data. The summit is holding the theoretical probability and the observed frequency side by side and explaining the gap as random variation in a finite number of trials. Students who stall here usually cannot write a part-to-whole fraction from a described group or move between fractions and decimals, gaps that reach back to grades 3 and 4. Intervention should rebuild part-of-a-set fractions and decimal notation first, then the grade 6 skills of part-to-whole ratios with scaling and fraction-decimal comparison, and only then return to probability language.

steps.rationale: The first modeling move: when outcomes are equally likely, assign each the same probability, 1/n, and check the model sums to 1. Everything downstream reads or builds a model.
Read a given model to find the probability of an event by ADDING the probabilities of the outcomes in it. The 'or' event adds -- the most common early error is multiplying.
Build the probability of an event from a sample space of counts: favorable over the total in the whole bag. This is the theoretical probability the rest of the standard predicts and compares against.
Create a model from a sample space and USE it -- multiply the probability by the number of trials to predict a count. This is the standard's 'predict the approximate relative frequency' demand.
Report what actually happened: experimental probability is the observed count over the number of trials. Separating observed from theoretical is required before the two can be compared.
The standard's summit: place the theoretical probability next to the experimental frequency, judge the agreement, and explain the discrepancy as random variation in a finite sample.

skills.name: Name the fraction of a set that has a given feature

prerequisite_skill.description: Write the fraction of a group of objects that has a certain feature, with the whole group as the denominator.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A group has 3 squares and 7 circles. What fraction of the shapes are squares?

skills.i_do_script: A fraction of a set counts part of a group over the WHOLE group. Watch: a tray holds 3 squares and 7 circles, so there are 10 shapes in all. The fraction of the shapes that are squares is 3 out of 10, written 3/10. The bottom is every shape on the tray, not just the circles. I lay the shapes in one row, count the whole row for the bottom, and count the squares for the top.

canonical_error.pattern: Writes the part over the OTHER part instead of over the whole group
canonical_error.example: For 3 squares and 7 circles, writes 3/7 instead of 3/10
canonical_error.why: The student compares squares to circles instead of squares to the whole set. The denominator of a fraction of a set is the count of everything in the group.

skills.item_template: A small group of objects described by counts. Student writes the fraction of the group with a named feature, part over whole. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: 5 of the 8 counters in a row are red. What fraction of the counters are red?
A group has 3 squares and 7 circles. What fraction of the shapes are squares?
4 of the 9 apples in a basket are green. What fraction of the apples are green?
A box holds 10 crayons and 3 of them are blue. What fraction of the crayons are blue?
2 of the 6 balloons are yellow. What fraction of the balloons are yellow?
A team has 5 girls and 4 boys. What fraction of the team are girls?
7 of the 12 eggs in a carton are brown. What fraction of the eggs are brown?
All 6 buttons in a jar are round. What fraction of the buttons are round?

redirect_script.stop: Did you count the WHOLE group for the bottom?
redirect_script.prompt: Lay the whole group in one row and count every object: that number goes on the bottom. Then count just the ones you want for the top. 3 squares out of 10 shapes is 3/10, not 3/7.
redirect_script.praise: You counted the whole group for the bottom, that is what makes it a fraction of the set.

vocabulary.definition: A part of a group of objects written over the count of the whole group.
Every object in the collection; its count goes on the bottom of the fraction.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 fractions of one whole with fraction circles (equal parts of a single shape) before returning to fractions of a set.

worked_example_script.text: Lay 3 square tiles and 7 circle tiles in one row of 10.
How many tiles are in the whole row? How many are squares?
10 tiles in all and 3 are squares, so the fraction of the tiles that are squares is 3/10. The bottom counts the whole row, squares included.
If a student writes 3/7, point at the row: did you count every tile for the bottom, or only the circles?
Your turn: a row has 2 yellow and 4 green cubes. What fraction of the cubes are yellow?

skills.name: Write tenths and hundredths as decimals

prerequisite_skill.description: Write a fraction with denominator 10 or 100 as a decimal, and read a decimal back as tenths or hundredths.

skills.i_do_script: A decimal is another name for tenths and hundredths. Watch: 3/10 means 3 tenths, and the tenths place is the first spot after the point, so 3/10 = 0.3. Now 27/100 means 27 hundredths: 2 tenths and 7 hundredths, so 27/100 = 0.27. Be careful with 7/100: that is only 7 hundredths, so a zero holds the tenths place and it is 0.07, not 0.7. On a hundredths grid, 0.7 shades 70 squares but 0.07 shades only 7.

canonical_error.pattern: Drops the numerator right after the decimal point no matter what the denominator is
canonical_error.why: The student ignores whether the fraction names tenths or hundredths. Hundredths need two places after the point, so 7 hundredths is 0.07 and a zero must hold the empty tenths place.

skills.item_template: A fraction with denominator 10 or 100, or a decimal to the hundredths. Student converts between the two forms or compares two values. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Write 3/10 as a decimal.
Write 27/100 as a decimal.
Write 7/100 as a decimal.
Write 0.9 as a fraction.
Write 6/10 as a decimal.
Write 0.03 as a fraction.
Which is greater: 0.3 or 0.07?
Write 40/100 as a decimal.

redirect_script.stop: Is that fraction tenths or hundredths?
redirect_script.prompt: Tenths use one place after the point and hundredths use two. 7/100 is 7 hundredths, so write a zero in the tenths place: 0.07. Check it on the grid: 7 squares, not 70.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the denominator to the right place, that is exactly how decimals work.

vocabulary.definition: The first place after the decimal point; one tenth is 1/10 or 0.1.
The second place after the decimal point; one hundredth is 1/100 or 0.01.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 tenths and hundredths with a hundredths grid (shade the fraction, then read the shading as a decimal).

worked_example_script.text: Shade 27 squares of a hundredths grid. Write 27/100 beside it.
How many full columns of ten are shaded? How many extra squares?
2 full columns is 2 tenths and 7 extra squares is 7 hundredths, so 27/100 = 0.27. The first place counts columns of ten, the second place counts single squares.
If a student writes 7/100 as 0.7, send them to the grid: does 7/100 shade 7 squares or 70?
Your turn: write 9/100 as a decimal.

skills.name: Write part-to-whole ratios and scale them with equivalent ratios

prerequisite_skill.description: Write the ratio of a part to the whole group and use equivalent ratios to find the part at a new total.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles. What is the ratio of red marbles to ALL the marbles?

skills.i_do_script: A part-to-whole ratio compares one kind of thing to the whole collection. Watch: a bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles, 10 in all, so the ratio of red to all marbles is 3 out of 10, written 3/10. That ratio is a rate I can scale: 3 out of every 10 means 6 out of every 20 and 9 out of every 30, because I multiply the part and the whole by the same number. The whole always rides on the bottom, and both numbers grow together.

canonical_error.pattern: Writes the part over the other part instead of over the whole, or scales only one number of the ratio
canonical_error.example: For 3 red and 7 blue, writes red to all as 3/7; or scales 3 out of 10 to 9 out of 10 for 30 marbles
canonical_error.why: The student either compares part to part when the question asks part to whole, or stretches the part without stretching the whole. A ratio keeps its value only when both numbers are multiplied by the same factor.

skills.item_template: A group described by counts, or a rate like 3 out of every 10. Student writes the part-to-whole ratio or scales it to a new total. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A class has 4 left-handed and 16 right-handed students. What is the ratio of left-handed students to ALL students?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4/20 = 1/5. Writing 4/16 compares part to part instead of part to whole.

sample_items.stem: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles. Write the ratio of red marbles to all the marbles.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3/10. Writing 3/7 uses the blue marbles as the whole.

sample_items.stem: 2 out of every 5 raffle tickets win a prize. At that rate, how many winners are in 20 tickets?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Scale by 4: 2 x 4 = 8 winners out of 5 x 4 = 20. Answering 2 ignores the scaling.

sample_items.stem: 3 out of 10 spins land on green. At the same rate, how many greens would there be in 50 spins?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Scale by 5: 3 x 5 = 15. Answering 3 or 43 misses the equivalent ratio.

sample_items.stem: A recipe box holds 5 dinner cards and 3 dessert cards. What fraction of the cards are dessert cards?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3/8. Writing 3/5 compares dessert to dinner.

sample_items.stem: 1 out of every 4 students walks to school. At that rate, how many walkers are in a school of 28 students?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Scale by 7: 1 x 7 = 7 out of 4 x 7 = 28.

sample_items.stem: A tray has 6 bran muffins and 6 corn muffins. Write the ratio of bran muffins to all the muffins.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 6/12 = 1/2. Writing 6/6 compares the two parts.

sample_items.stem: 4 out of 6 seeds sprout. Write an equivalent ratio with a whole of 30 seeds.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Multiply both numbers by 5. Writing 4 out of 30 scales the whole but not the part.

redirect_script.stop: Is the bottom the whole group, and did BOTH numbers scale?
redirect_script.prompt: Add the parts to find the whole first, then write part over whole. When you scale, multiply the part and the whole by the same number: 3 out of 10 becomes 9 out of 30, not 9 out of 10.
redirect_script.praise: You kept the whole on the bottom and stretched both numbers together, that is ratio reasoning.

vocabulary.definition: A comparison of one part of a group to the entire group, like 3 red out of 10 marbles.
Ratios that name the same rate, made by multiplying or dividing both numbers by the same factor.
A ratio read as 'out of every,' like 3 out of every 10 spins.

worked_example_script.text: Lay a row of 10 cubes: 3 red and 7 blue. Under it, lay three copies of the same row to make 30 cubes.
In one row, what is the ratio of red to ALL the cubes? What happens to the reds when we lay 3 rows?
One row is 3 red out of 10. Three rows is 9 red out of 30, the same rate, because every row carries its own 3 reds. Part and whole grew by the same factor.
If a student says 3 out of 7, ask whether the red cubes belong to the row. The whole row, reds included, goes on the bottom.
Your turn: 2 out of every 5 tickets win. At that rate, how many winners in 20 tickets?

practice_problems.stem: A bag has 2 red and 3 blue marbles. How many marbles are in the whole bag?
For that bag, write the ratio of red marbles to ALL the marbles.
A class has 4 left-handed and 16 right-handed students. What fraction of the class is left-handed?
3 out of every 10 spins land on green. At that rate, how many greens in 40 spins?
A box has 5 pencils and 7 pens. Write the ratio of pens to all the items.
1 out of every 6 rolls shows a four. At that rate, how many fours in 42 rolls?
4 out of 6 seeds sprout. Write equivalent ratios with wholes of 30 seeds and 60 seeds.
Leo wrote the ratio of red marbles to all the marbles for a bag with 3 red and 7 blue. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Leo compared red to blue. The whole bag has 3 + 7 = 10 marbles, so red to all is 3/10.

activities.title: Rows That Repeat the Rate
activities.instructions:
1. Build one row that shows a rate, like 2 red out of 5 cubes.
2. Write the part-to-whole ratio for the row: 2/5.
3. Build more identical rows until the whole reaches 20 cubes, then count the reds.
4. Write the equivalent ratio: 8 out of 20, and say what factor both numbers grew by.
5. Repeat with 3 red out of 10 scaled to 30. Say each time: the whole goes on the bottom, and both numbers grow together.

activities.title: Same Rate Match-Up
materials: Card deck: one card per starting ratio, one card per scaled ratio
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each starting ratio like 3 out of 10 to its scaled twin like 15 out of 50.
3. To claim a match, say the factor both numbers were multiplied by.
4. Two decoy cards scale only one number; set them aside and explain what went wrong.

strategy_links.why: Repeating a physical row of counters makes 'both numbers grow by the same factor' visible before the equivalent-ratio rule is named.
The part-to-part denominator and the scale-one-number bug are stable, baitable errors ideal for find-and-fix work.
Think-pair-share on 'which number is the whole?' surfaces the part-to-whole decision before students commit an answer.

questioning_prompts: What is the whole group here, and how do you find its count?
Is this question part to part or part to whole?
What factor takes the whole from 10 to 40? What does that do to the part?
Why must both numbers of the ratio be multiplied by the same factor?
Could the part ever be bigger than the whole? What would that mean?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes the part over the other part, like 3/7 for 3 red and 7 blue.
misconception_redirects.say: Add the parts first: 3 + 7 = 10 is the whole bag. Red to ALL is 3/10. Point at the row: do the red cubes belong to the group too?
misconception_redirects.praise: You put the whole group on the bottom, that keeps the ratio part to whole.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student scales the whole but leaves the part alone, like 3 out of 30 from 3 out of 10.
misconception_redirects.say: Every row of 10 carries its own 3 reds. Three rows means 3 x 3 = 9 reds out of 30. Multiply both numbers by the same factor.
misconception_redirects.praise: You stretched the part and the whole together, so the rate stayed the same.

quick_checks.prompt: A jar has 2 red and 8 green beads. Ratio of red to all beads?
quick_checks.look_for: 2/10 = 1/5. An answer of 2/8 compares part to part.

quick_checks.prompt: 3 out of every 10 spins land green. How many greens in 30 spins?
quick_checks.look_for: 9, from multiplying both numbers by 3. An answer of 3 means no scaling happened.

worked_solution.stem: A bag has 3 red and 9 blue marbles. Write the ratio of red marbles to all the marbles, then find how many reds you would expect at the same rate in a bag of 40 marbles.

steps.annotation: Add the parts to find the whole bag.
Part over whole, then reduce: 1 red out of every 4 marbles.
The new whole is 10 times the reduced whole of 4.
Scale the part by the same factor of 10.

faded_example.stem: A bag has 2 red and 8 blue marbles. Write the ratio of red to all the marbles, then find how many reds you would expect at the same rate in a bag of 35 marbles.

steps.annotation: Add the parts to find the whole.
Part over whole, reduced: 1 out of every 5.
Find the factor that takes the whole from 5 to 35.
Scale the part by that same factor to get the reds.

sentence_starters: The whole group has ___ items, so the ratio of ___ to all is ___/___.
Both numbers were multiplied by ___, so ___ out of ___ equals ___ out of ___.

skills.name: Write fractions as decimals and compare the two forms

prerequisite_skill.description: Convert a fraction to a decimal by dividing or renaming, and compare values given in mixed forms.

skills.i_do_script: A fraction and a decimal can name the same number, and dividing gets me from one to the other. Watch: 1/4 means 1 divided by 4, which is 0.25; I can also rename 1/4 as 25/100. To compare 0.3 with 1/4, I put both in decimal form: 0.30 against 0.25, and 30 hundredths beats 25 hundredths, so 0.3 is greater. Some fractions do not stop, like 1/6 = 0.1666..., so I round to the nearest hundredth and write about 0.17.

canonical_error.pattern: Builds the decimal from the fraction's digits instead of dividing or renaming
canonical_error.example: Writes 1/5 as 0.15 or as 0.5 instead of dividing to get 0.2
canonical_error.why: The student copies the numerator and denominator into decimal places instead of finding the value. A fraction is a division: 1/5 means 1 divided by 5, which is 0.2, and only that value lines up on the number line.

skills.item_template: A fraction with a small denominator, or a fraction and a decimal to compare. Student converts by dividing or renaming, rounding to the hundredth when needed. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: Write 1/4 as a decimal.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1 divided by 4 = 0.25. Writing 0.14 copies the digits instead of dividing.

sample_items.stem: Write 3/5 as a decimal.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3/5 = 6/10 = 0.6. Writing 0.35 copies the digits.

sample_items.stem: Which is greater: 0.3 or 1/4?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 0.30 vs 0.25, so 0.3 wins. Choosing 1/4 often comes from comparing the 4 to the 3.

sample_items.stem: Write 7/10 as a decimal.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 7 tenths is 0.7.

sample_items.stem: Write 1/6 as a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1 divided by 6 = 0.1666..., which rounds to 0.17. Writing 0.16 truncates instead of rounding.

sample_items.stem: Which is greater: 2/5 or 0.35?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2/5 = 0.40, which beats 0.35.

sample_items.stem: Write 9/20 as a decimal.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9/20 = 45/100 = 0.45. Writing 0.92 copies the digits.

sample_items.stem: Order from least to greatest: 0.5, 2/5, 0.45.

redirect_script.stop: Did you divide, or just copy the digits?
redirect_script.prompt: A fraction is a division: top divided by bottom. 1/5 is 1 divided by 5, which is 0.2. Then compare decimals place by place, adding zeros so both show hundredths.
redirect_script.praise: You found the value by dividing, so both numbers landed on the same ruler.

vocabulary.definition: A fraction and a decimal that name the same number, like 1/4 and 0.25.
A decimal whose digits repeat forever, like 1/6 = 0.1666..., often rounded for use.
Replace a number with the nearest value at a given place, like 0.1666... to 0.17.

worked_example_script.text: Shade 1/4 of a hundredths grid by splitting the grid into 4 equal blocks and shading one block.
How many small squares did that one block shade? So what decimal names 1/4?
One block of the four is 25 squares, so 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25. Dividing 1 by 4 gives the same 0.25. Now 0.3 shades 30 squares, so 0.3 is greater than 1/4.
If a student writes 1/4 = 0.14, send them to the grid: does 1/4 shade 14 squares? Divide instead of copying digits.
Your turn: which is greater, 0.45 or 2/5?

practice_problems.stem: Write 1/2 as a decimal.
Write 3/10 as a decimal.
Write 3/4 as a decimal.
Which is greater: 0.6 or 1/2?
Write 2/3 as a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
Which is greater: 3/5 or 0.55?
Order from least to greatest: 1/4, 0.3, 1/5.
Mara converted 1/5 to a decimal. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: put the 1 and the 5 after the point
practice_problems.answer: She copied the digits instead of dividing. 1 divided by 5 = 0.2 (or 1/5 = 2/10 = 0.2), so 1/5 = 0.2, not 0.15.

activities.title: Grid the Fraction
activities.instructions:
1. Take a fraction card like 1/4, 2/5, or 3/4.
2. Split a hundredths grid into that many equal blocks and shade the fraction.
3. Count the shaded squares and write the decimal, like 25 squares for 0.25.
4. Check by dividing top by bottom on the calculator; the decimal should match the count.
5. Say each time: the fraction and the decimal shade the exact same squares.

activities.title: Same Number, Two Names
materials: Card deck of fractions and decimals
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Pair each fraction with the decimal that names the same number.
3. To claim a pair, show the division or the renaming out loud.
4. Two decoy decimals were made by copying digits; set them aside and explain the trap.
5. Finish by ordering all the pairs from least to greatest on one line.

cards.text: 0.15 (copied from 1/5)
0.34 (copied from 3/4)

strategy_links.why: Shading the fraction on a hundredths grid and reading the same squares as a decimal makes the equivalence concrete before division is named.
The copied-digits decimal is a precise, baitable error that find-and-fix confronts directly.
Thinking aloud 'the fraction bar means divide' models the decision students skip when they copy digits.

questioning_prompts: What division does the fraction bar tell you to do?
How many hundredths does this fraction shade on the grid?
Before you compare, are both numbers in the same form?
Why do we add a zero to 0.3 before comparing it to 0.25?
When the division never stops, what do you do with the decimal?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes the fraction's digits straight into decimal places, like 1/5 = 0.15.
misconception_redirects.say: The fraction bar means divide: 1 divided by 5 is 0.2. Check the grid: 1/5 shades 20 squares, not 15.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided to find the value instead of copying digits.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student compares a fraction and a decimal without converting, judging by the size of the digits.
misconception_redirects.say: Put both numbers in decimal form first, then compare place by place. 1/4 is 0.25, and 0.30 beats 0.25.
misconception_redirects.praise: You moved both numbers to the same form before comparing, that makes the comparison fair.

quick_checks.look_for: 0.4. An answer of 0.25 or 0.52 means digits were copied instead of divided.
2/5, because it equals 0.40. Choosing 0.35 means no conversion happened.

steps.annotation: The fraction bar means divide the top by the bottom.
Add zeros so both numbers show the same places.
Tenths first: 4 tenths beats 3 tenths.
So 0.4 is the greater number.
Divide the top by the bottom.
Add zeros so both show thousandths.
Compare the two decimals place by place.
State which original number is greater.

sentence_starters: The fraction ___/___ means ___ divided by ___, which is ___.
In decimal form the numbers are ___ and ___, so ___ is greater.

skills.name: Build a uniform probability model for equally likely outcomes
skills.i_do_script: When every outcome is equally likely, each one has the SAME probability: 1 divided by the number of outcomes. Watch a spinner with 5 equal-sized sections, each a different color. There are 5 equally likely outcomes, so each color has a probability of 1/5. I fill the whole model with 1/5, 1/5, 1/5, 1/5, 1/5 -- and as a check, they add up to 5/5 = 1, because SOMETHING always happens.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses the outcome NUMBER (like 1/1, 1/2, 1/3...) instead of 1 over the total number of outcomes
canonical_error.example: For a 5-section spinner writes P = 1/1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 for the five colors instead of 1/5 for every color
canonical_error.why: The student counts outcomes one at a time and lets the count creep into the denominator. In a uniform model every equally likely outcome shares the SAME probability, 1/n, where n is the total number of outcomes.

skills.item_template: A description of n equally likely outcomes (equal spinner sections, a fair cube, identical tiles). Student states the probability of each outcome. Short response.

sample_items.stem: A spinner has 5 equal-sized sections, each a different color. What is the probability of landing on each color?
A fair number cube is numbered 1 through 6. What is the probability of each outcome?
A bag holds 4 identical tiles, each printed with a different letter. What is the probability of drawing each letter?
A spinner has 8 equal sections. What is the probability of landing on any one given section?
A model for a fair coin lists heads and tails. What probability goes with each?

redirect_script.stop: Are the sections the same size? Then same probability?
redirect_script.prompt: Every equal section has the SAME probability: 1 over the total number of sections. For 5 equal sections that is 1/5 for each -- not 1/1, 1/2, 1/3...
redirect_script.praise: You gave every equal outcome the same 1/n -- that is a uniform model.

vocabulary.definition: A model where every outcome is equally likely, so each has probability 1/n.
Outcomes that all have the same chance of happening.
A list of every outcome with its probability; the probabilities add to 1.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, blue, green, yellow. Build the model.'
How many equally likely outcomes are there? So what is each one's probability?
4 equal outcomes, so each is 1/4: red 1/4, blue 1/4, green 1/4, yellow 1/4. They add to 4/4 = 1.
If a student writes 1/1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, ask 'are the sections the same size? Then shouldn't they have the SAME probability?'
Your turn: a fair number cube 1-6 -- what is the probability of each face?

practice_problems.stem: A spinner has 4 equal sections. How many equally likely outcomes are there?
If 3 outcomes are equally likely, what is the probability of each?
A spinner has 5 equal-sized sections, each a different color. Give the probability of each color.
A fair number cube is numbered 1-6. Build the probability model for the six outcomes.
Sam built a model for a spinner with 4 equal sections. Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Every equal section has the SAME probability: 1/4 each. The four should be 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, which add to 4/4 = 1. Sam's add to more than 2.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: counting outcomes into the denominator.

practice_problems.stem: A bag has 10 identical tiles, each a different number 1-10. What is the probability of drawing any one particular number?
A uniform model gives each outcome a probability of 1/7. How many equally likely outcomes are there, and what do all the probabilities add up to?
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: from 1/n back to n; the sum is 1.

practice_problems.stem: A student says a spinner with 3 equal sections has probabilities 1/3, 1/3, and 1/2. Explain why this cannot be a correct model.
practice_problems.answer: The probabilities must add to 1. 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/2 = 7/6, which is more than 1, so the model is impossible; each should be 1/3.
practice_problems.notes: Uses the sum-to-1 check to reject a bad model.

activities.title: Uniform or Not?
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each card into 'Equally likely (use 1/n)' or 'Not equally likely.'
2. For every 'equally likely' card, write the probability of one outcome as 1/n.
3. For a 'not equally likely' card, explain in one phrase why the outcomes are not the same.
4. Debrief: what has to be true before you can use 1/n for every outcome?

cards.text: A fair coin: heads or tails
A spinner with 5 equal sections
A bag with 3 red and 1 blue marble
A fair number cube 1-6
A spinner with one big half and two small quarters
8 identical lettered tiles
A weighted die that lands on 6 more often
4 equal-size slices, each a different flavor

activities.title: Every Section the Same
activities.instructions:
1. Read Sam's model: red 1/1, blue 1/2, green 1/3, yellow 1/4.
2. Add Sam's four fractions -- what do they total? Should a model total that much?
3. Rebuild the model so every equal section has the same probability.
4. Write the rule: for n equal outcomes, each is ____ and they add to ____.

content.worked_problem: A spinner has 4 equal sections. Sam wrote red 1/1, blue 1/2, green 1/3, yellow 1/4.
content.error_step: Sam let the outcome number become the denominator instead of using the total, 4.
content.why: Equal sections share one probability, 1/4 each, and 4 x 1/4 = 1. Sam's fractions add to far more than 1.

strategy_links.why: Coloring equal spinner sections and then labeling each one 1/n moves students from the picture to the symbolic uniform model.
A quick choral 'one over the number of sections' builds automaticity for assigning 1/n to equally likely outcomes.
The 'number the outcomes into the denominator' bug is clean and baitable with find-and-fix plus a sum-to-1 check.

questioning_prompts: How many equally likely outcomes are there?

skills.i_do_script: The sample space is the whole bag laid out in one row -- every ball gets its own square, and the draw can land on any square in that row. skills.i_do_script: This skill has two moves: build the model, then predict. Watch a box with 3 blue, 5 purple, 2 orange, 5 black marbles, 15 total. skills.i_do_script: Experimental probability is what ACTUALLY happened: the observed count of an event over the number of trials you ran. skills.name: Compare experimental frequency to the theoretical model and explain discrepancy
skills.i_do_script: Now I put the two probabilities side by side. Watch a fair number cube rolled 60 times; a 3 came up 8 times. The THEORETICAL probability of a 3 is 1/6, about 0.17. The EXPERIMENTAL probability is 8/60, about 0.13. They're close but not equal, and that's expected: probability predicts BEFORE the experiment, but any finite number of rolls has random ups and downs. A gap doesn't mean the cube is unfair -- it usually means the sample was small.

canonical_error.pattern: Concludes the cube or spinner is unfair (or the model is wrong) because the observed frequency does not exactly match the theoretical probability
canonical_error.example: Observed 8 threes in 60 rolls instead of the expected 10, so the student says the cube is rigged, rather than citing normal random variation
canonical_error.why: The student expects experimental results to match the theoretical model exactly. In a finite number of trials, random variation makes small gaps normal; the model is a long-run prediction, not a guarantee for each run.

skills.item_template: A theoretical model and observed results (given as text). Student finds both probabilities, compares them, and explains the difference. Multi-part / explanation response.

sample_items.stem: A fair number cube (1-6) is rolled 60 times; a 3 comes up 8 times. Part A: What is the theoretical probability of rolling a 3? Part B: How does the experimental frequency compare, and what might explain any difference?
sample_items.answer: Part A: 1/6 (about 0.17). Part B: experimental is 8/60 = about 0.13, a little less than 1/6; the small gap is normal random variation in 60 rolls, not an unfair cube.

sample_items.stem: A fair coin is flipped 40 times and lands heads 24 times. Part A: theoretical probability of heads? Part B: compare to the experimental frequency and explain.
sample_items.answer: Part A: 1/2 = 0.5. Part B: experimental is 24/40 = 0.6, a bit higher than 0.5; the difference is due to random chance in a finite number of flips.

sample_items.stem: A spinner has 4 equal sections. It is spun 40 times and red comes up 12 times. Part A: theoretical P(red)? Part B: compare and explain.
sample_items.answer: Part A: 1/4 = 0.25. Part B: experimental is 12/40 = 0.3, close to 0.25; the small difference reflects random variation, and more spins would likely bring them closer.

sample_items.stem: A fair number cube is rolled 30 times; a 5 comes up 4 times. Part A: theoretical P(5)? Part B: compare and explain.
sample_items.answer: Part A: 1/6 (about 0.17). Part B: experimental is 4/30 = about 0.13, a bit below 1/6; a 30-roll sample is small, so random chance easily explains the gap.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3, writing the probability of an event as favorable over total from a sample space, the At-proficiency workhorse the rest of the standard predicts and compares against. If they pass, push up to S4 (build a model and predict a count) and S6 (compare theoretical to experimental and explain the gap). If they fail, drop one grade to the new Looking Back pair: B1 checks part-to-whole ratios with scaling, the grade 6 engine under every favorable-over-total and prediction move, and B2 checks fraction-decimal conversion, which the comparison work leans on. If those wobble, the foundations locate the gap further down: F1 (fraction of a set, grade 3) and F2 (tenths and hundredths as decimals, grade 4). S1, S2, and S5 remain available to probe the standard's own model-building, model-reading, and experimental threads.
